implementation_notes: The browser and Node expose Atomics for SharedArrayBuffer: load, store, add, sub, and, since ES2024, compareExchange and wait/notify. These are genuinely hardware atomics over shared memory and are what worker_threads coordination is built on. Atomics.wait is disallowed on the browser main thread (it would block the UI), so a main-thread worker cannot spin-wait; the usual pattern is to post the work to a worker and let the worker's wait do the blocking. Without SharedArrayBuffer there is no hardware atomic in JavaScript at all - the single-threaded event loop is what makes ordinary code safe, and structured concurrency via promises is the answer. Atomics operations on a non-shared ArrayBuffer are simply sequential.
pitfalls: Atomics.wait is forbidden on the browser main thread and throws - blocking the UI is never acceptable, so the wait must happen in a worker.
SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers); without it the constructor is unavailable, which makes this pattern unusable in many deployed pages.
Every Atomics operation is sequentially consistent; there is no acquire/release, so a hot counter overpays and there is no way to express a weaker order.
A regular Array instead of an Int32Array has no Atomics support and silently falls back to sequential semantics.
